CausalChain: SF3B2 upregulation -> SF3B2/SRSF1 cooperative binding alters splicing of integrase cofactors and DNA repair regulators -> Generation of pro-integrative and DNA repair-deficient isoforms -> Enhanced viral DNA integration -> Localized genomic instability -> Activation of oncogenic pathways (metastasis, angiogenesis)
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in hepatitis virus–associated liver neoplasms, the upregulation of SF3B2 in concert with SRSF1 leads to a targeted alternative splicing shift in a select group of integrase cofactors and DNA repair regulators. This shift results in the production of splice variants that both promote viral DNA integration and undermine genomic maintenance mechanisms, thereby creating optimized conditions for integration-induced genomic instability. Such instability then acts as a driving force for oncogenic signaling pathways involved in metastasis and angiogenesis. This refined view builds upon the original hypothesis by not only positing a mechanistic bridge between splicing factor dysregulation and viral integration, but also by utilizing precision technologies—CRISPR-Cas9, long-read RNA-seq, and single-cell assays—to dissect and temporally validate each step of this process.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly those linked to hepatitis viruses, features widespread dysregulation of alternative splicing. We propose that upregulation of the splicing factor SF3B2, in close cooperation with SRSF1, specifically redirects alternative splicing of key integrase cofactors and DNA repair regulators, thereby creating a cellular milieu that favors viral DNA integration. This SF3B2/SRSF1-driven splicing shift not only impairs normal DNA repair mechanisms but also increases the production of splice variants that boost integrase functionality, leading to localized genomic instability and the activation of oncogenic pathways such as metastasis and angiogenesis. To interrogate this refined causal relationship, we will use contemporary technologies including CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing to modulate SF3B2/SRSF1 expression, long-read RNA sequencing to resolve complex splicing isoforms, and single-cell viral integration assays. This strategy aims to disentangle the contributions of precise splicing events from the broader landscape of splicing dysregulation observed in HCC and to firmly establish a molecular link between splicing alterations and oncogenesis.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis broadly suggested that upregulated SF3B2, working with SRSF1, causes splicing alterations in integrase cofactors and DNA repair regulators leading to viral integration and genomic instability. The revised hypothesis refines this by specifying that SF3B2/SRSF1 cooperate to generate specific splice variants that enhance integrase activity and reduce DNA repair capability. It further addresses gaps by identifying the necessity to distinguish this mechanism from general splicing dysregulation, specifying the molecular targets, and detailing downstream oncogenic outcomes. Contemporary technologies such as CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, long-read RNA sequencing, and single-cell assays are explicitly integrated to more precisely test each critical step of the original causal chain.
